title: Laughing in Indonesian
goal: Understand — and eventually tell — Indonesian jokes: riddles built on sound and double meaning (*tebak-tebakan*), twisted proverbs (*plesetan*) and the humorous *pantun jenaka*. Also learn the words for when a joke works (*ngakak*) and when it doesn't (*garing*).
bekal: get the joke in a *tebak-tebakan* by spotting the sound-alike or the double meaning: *lele-lawar*, *motor bebek*
recognise a *plesetan* and name the original: *ada udang di balik rempeyek*
read a *pantun jenaka*, separate *sampiran* from *isi*, and react to humour: *garing*, *receh*, *ngakak*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Tebak-tebakan saat makan siang
dialogs.intro: August, a scorching Friday. Nobody wants to go out in the midday heat, so Sarah, Fajar and Yoga eat nasi bungkus in the office pantry, and Fajar starts his weekly riddle session.

notes: **Tebak-tebakan** — riddles — follow a fixed frame: *X, X apa yang…?* (“X, what X…?”). The repeated noun is the signal that a pun is coming, and the answer is never a real fact. That is why Sarah's sincere *Ikan terbang kan memang ada* is, for Fajar and Yoga, the funniest line of the lunch.

**Garing** literally means “dry and crisp”, like crackers; of a joke it means it fell flat. Yoga extends the metaphor with *kriuk-kriuk kayak kerupuk* (crunchy like a prawn cracker). Other ways to say the same: *jayus* (trying too hard and failing) and *krik krik*, the sound of crickets in the silence.

**Plesetan** (standard spelling *pelesetan*) comes from *peleset*, “to slip”: a word or phrase deliberately made to slip into another. It is the engine of Indonesian humour, from riddles to song parodies to protest banners. The verb is *memelesetkan*; in Jakarta, *diplesetin*.

**Motor bebek** — a “duck bike” — is the step-through motorcycle that fills Indonesian roads, named for its round, squat shape. Locking the steering (*kunci stang*) turns the handlebars fully to the left, so a “bebek with a locked steering” can only waddle round in circles. A double meaning plus local knowledge: a perfect *tebak-tebakan*.

💬 **Bang** is short for *abang*, Betawi for “older brother”. Yoga uses it for Fajar the way a Javanese speaker would say *Mas*. *Gantian* (“take turns; my turn”), *diselipin* (= *diselipkan*, slipped in) and *dijelasin* (= *dijelaskan*) are everyday Jakarta forms.

**Loading** and **telat ketawa** — laughing late — are a friendly tease, not an insult. The Indonesian slang word for “slow on the uptake” is *lemot*. Sarah's answer, *otak saya masih menerjemahkan*, is the right move: make fun of yourself first and the teasing loses its sting.

grammars.title: How the jokes work
body: Indonesian riddles run on a handful of mechanisms. Once you can name the mechanism, you can decode new riddles — and build your own.

head: Mechanism
Riddle
The trick
rows: *Bebek apa yang jalannya ke kiri terus?*
*Kenapa di baju Superman ada huruf S? — Kalau M, kebesaran.*
the S read as a clothing size
*Kenapa ayam jago berkokok sambil merem? — Sudah hafal teksnya.*

after: The last one is the cleverest: *rempeyek* is a crispy cracker with little shrimps or peanuts stuck in it, so the plesetan is literally true. Good plesetan often work that way — the twist lands somewhere real.

grammars.title: Talking about humour
body: Most words for humour live in casual speech. Here they are with the standard form where one exists, so you can recognise both.

head: Casual
Standard
English
rows: silly, cheap (humour), in a fond way
to make a dig, be sarcastic

after: *Humor receh* (small-change humour) is not an insult; many people proudly call their own taste *receh* — they laugh at everything. *Jangan baper!* (“don't take it personally!”) is what people say right after a tease has gone slightly too far.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Malam komedi
dialogs.intro: Saturday night at a small stand-up venue in South Jakarta. Mbak Dewi, the journalist from Unit 6, has become a friend and dragged Sarah along. They talk on the way out.

lines.text: Nah, itu lucu! Kalau kamu udah bisa ngelawak kayak gitu, bahasamu udah naik kelas.

lines.text: Jangan dimuat di korannya, ya, Wi. Nanti judulnya “Bule Belajar Melawak”.

notes: **Komika** is the Indonesian word for a stand-up comedian, coined when stand-up boomed in the early 2010s. The older tradition is the *pelawak* — sketch and slapstick comedians from troupes like Srimulat — and their craft is *lawakan*. A night of stand-up is *malam komedi* or simply *open mic*.

**Mertua and macet** are the twin pillars of Indonesian observational comedy. In-law jokes land because many couples live with or near their parents-in-law; traffic jokes land because everybody has lost three hours to Jakarta's roads that week.

**Numpang lewat** — “just passing through” (literally “hitching a ride past”) — is how you say something arrived and left almost at once. It applies to salaries, to a celebrity at a wedding, to the sun in rainy season. *Numpang* on its own is “to hitch, to borrow space”: *Numpang tanya* (may I ask?), *numpang ke toilet*.

**Tanggal tua and tanggal muda.** Literally “old date” and “young date”: the end of the month, when money is tight, and just after payday (*gajian*), when it isn't. Restaurants run *promo tanggal tua*; nobody has ever run *promo tanggal muda*.

**Bule** is the everyday word for a white foreigner, from *bulai* (albino). It is usually neutral or even affectionate, but it is a label, and some foreigners dislike being called it. Sarah using it about herself is self-deprecating and lands well; don't use it about someone in a formal setting.

**Naik kelas** — “go up a class” at school — is used figuratively for any promotion in status or skill: *bahasamu udah naik kelas*, *warung itu sudah naik kelas jadi restoran*. Its opposite, *tinggal kelas* (to repeat a year), is also used figuratively, less kindly.

grammars.title: Pantun jenaka, line by line
body: You wrote a pantun for Kinan in Unit 9. The *pantun jenaka* (humorous pantun) uses exactly the same form: four lines of eight to twelve syllables, rhyming a-b-a-b, with the joke saved for line 4.
after: Sampiran usually borrow a place name or an everyday errand — *Jalan-jalan ke Pasar Baru…*, *Pergi ke pasar membeli…* — because the rhyme is what matters, not the sense. The audience hears line 1, predicts the rhyme, and laughs when line 3 lands on it with something unexpected.
Comedians often end a set with a pantun because the form itself signals “this is the end, clap now” — exactly as *Demikian* did in Unit 13's sambutan.

blocks.text: These are classics; every Indonesian over the age of eight will know most of them. Tell one at an office lunch and you will be met with groans — which is the correct response.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Some riddles and a lot of old comedy play on ethnic accents or stereotypes. Indonesians call that territory *SARA* (*suku, agama, ras, antargolongan*: ethnicity, religion, race, social group), and in public it is best avoided entirely, however much the room seems to be laughing.
A plesetan only works if everyone knows the original, so these twisted proverbs double as a quick proverb lesson. The first two are well known; the others are the kind people make up on the spot.

head: Original
Plesetan
The original means
rows: united we stand, divided we fall
make do with what you have
there are many ways to succeed

blocks.text: Plesetan also attack acronyms and slogans. Any official abbreviation (Unit 8) is fair game for a new, less flattering expansion — which is why a new government acronym is usually mocked on social media within hours of being announced.
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.

head: English
Indonesian
rows: Mbak, I've pulled the data together. We've got loads more participants than in the first quarter.
*Mbak, datanya udah aku rekap. Pesertanya naik banyak banget dibanding triwulan pertama.*
Will do. And the teacher training? That one actually went down.
*Siap. Terus yang pelatihan guru, Mbak? Itu malah turun.*
Yes. Oh, one more thing: average participant satisfaction came out at 4.6 out of 5.
*Iya. Oh, satu lagi: rata-rata nilai kepuasan peserta tercatat 4.6 dari 5.*
The next chart shows participant numbers per month. As you can see, the trend is steadily upward.
*Grafik berikut menunjukkan jumlah peserta per bulan. Seperti terlihat, trennya terus meningkat.*
Will this decline continue into the second half of the year?
*Apakah penurunan ini akan berlanjut pada semester kedua?*
